title: Conduct Continuous Cleaning and Sanitising of the Abattoir

lessons.title: Keeping the small stock line clean during the shift
lessons.html:
Why clean all day

On a sheep and goat line, wool, hair, blood, fat, dung and stomach contents build up quickly. Wool sticks to everything and carries germs. If it lands on a carcass it must be trimmed off. Continuous cleaning during the shift keeps the line safe and hygienic.

What to clean during production

  • Floors: pick up wool, pieces of skin, fat and meat scraps and put them in the right bins. Push water and blood to the drains with a squeegee.
  • Skin chute and skin area: keep skins moving into the chute or bins; do not let them pile up near the line.
  • Platforms and work stands: rinse off blood and fat often so they are not slippery.
  • Hand-wash basins: keep soap and paper towels filled.
  • Knife sterilizers: check they are full and hot. Remove fat and wool from the water.
  • Bins: empty before they overflow. Keep condemned bins closed and marked.
  • Drains: clear wool from drain covers; wool blocks drains very fast.

Rules during production

  1. Never spray water where it can splash onto carcasses.
  2. Use low-pressure water only.
  3. Do not use chemicals near meat unless the procedure allows it.
  4. Use colour-coded tools: floor tools never touch food-contact surfaces.
  5. Warn workers before you clean near them.
  6. Never clean a moving machine or conveyor.

Good cleaning during the day means a faster, easier clean-up at the end.

lessons.title: The end-of-day clean
lessons.html:
Clean first, then sanitise

Cleaning removes visible dirt, wool, fat and blood. Sanitising kills most of the germs left behind. A sanitiser cannot work on a dirty surface, so you always clean first.

Step by step

  1. Prepare: all carcasses and offal must have left the area. Machines such as the skin puller, hoists and conveyors are switched off and locked out by an authorised person. Protect electrical boxes as the procedure says.
  2. Dry clean: scrape and pick up wool, skin pieces, fat and stomach contents. Clear drain covers.
  3. Pre-rinse: rinse with warm water from top to bottom: overhead rails and high equipment first, then walls and equipment, floors last.
  4. Apply detergent at the strength the label and procedure say. Leave it for the stated contact time.
  5. Scrub with brushes, especially on hooks, spreaders, trays, platforms, corners and under equipment.
  6. Rinse all detergent off, top to bottom.
  7. Inspect: no wool, fat, blood or film may be left. Clean again if needed.
  8. Sanitise food-contact surfaces with the correct sanitiser and strength. Rinse or leave on, as the label says.
  9. Finish: squeegee water to drains, put tools away clean, and sign the cleaning checklist.

Special items

  • Hooks and spreaders: washed and sanitised before reuse; some plants use a hook-washing machine.
  • Offal trays and containers: red offal and rough offal containers are cleaned separately.
  • Aprons and boots: washed at the apron and boot wash stations.

lessons.title: Chemical safety and checking your work
lessons.html:
Using cleaning chemicals safely

Abattoir detergents and sanitisers can burn skin and eyes. Treat them with care.

Always

  • Read the label or ask your supervisor to explain it and the safety data sheet (SDS).
  • Wear rubber gloves, goggles or a face shield, an apron and boots.
  • Measure exactly; use the dosing system if there is one.
  • Add chemical to water, never water to chemical.
  • Keep chemicals in labelled containers in the locked chemical store.

Never

  • Never mix chemicals. Some mixtures, such as chlorine and acid, give off poisonous gas.
  • Never use food or cool-drink containers for chemicals.
  • Never use more than the label says.
  • Never spray towards people.

Accidents

  • In the eye: rinse at the eye-wash station with lots of running water for a long time and call for help.
  • On the skin: remove wet clothing and rinse with plenty of water.
  • Report every accident and take the label or SDS to the clinic.

First aid must be learned in hands-on training by an accredited provider.

Checking your work

Before slaughter starts the next day, the supervisor or quality controller does a pre-operational check. They look at and feel surfaces and may take swabs. If something is not clean, it must be cleaned again before work starts. Take pride in passing this check first time.

Key points

  • Clean continuously during the shift; clear wool from floors and drains.
  • Never spray water near carcasses during production.
  • Always clean before you sanitise, working top to bottom.
  • Lock out machines before cleaning them.
  • Measure chemicals exactly, never mix them, and wear gloves and goggles.
  • Sign the cleaning checklist only after the work is done.
